questions.explanation: ADH stands for anti-diuretic hormone. 'Anti-diuretic' means it works against the production of dilute urine (diuresis), thereby helping the body retain water when it is dehydrated.

questions.stem: Where is ADH produced and released from?
questions.explanation: ADH is produced by the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary gland into the blood. It then travels to the kidneys where it acts on the collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption.

questions.stem: When a person is dehydrated, what happens to ADH levels?
questions.explanation: When dehydrated, the blood becomes more concentrated. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this and trigger increased ADH release from the pituitary gland. More ADH causes more water to be reabsorbed from the collecting duct.

questions.stem: What effect does ADH have on the collecting duct?

options.text: It causes active transport of urea
It makes the walls more permeable to water
It makes the walls less permeable to water
It increases the rate of ultrafiltration

questions.explanation: ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct walls to water by inserting aquaporins (water channels) into the cell membranes. This allows more water to be reabsorbed by osmosis, producing more concentrated urine.

questions.stem: A person drinks a large volume of water. What type of urine would they produce?

options.text: A small volume of dilute urine
A small volume of concentrated urine
A large volume of dilute urine

questions.explanation: After drinking lots of water, the blood becomes more dilute. ADH release decreases, making the collecting duct less permeable to water. Less water is reabsorbed, resulting in a large volume of dilute urine being produced.

questions.stem: Which cells detect changes in blood water concentration?
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in blood water concentration (osmolarity). When the blood becomes too concentrated, they trigger ADH release; when it becomes too dilute, they reduce ADH release.

questions.stem: The control of water balance by ADH is an example of which biological mechanism?
questions.explanation: Water balance is controlled by negative feedback. A change in water levels is detected, ADH release is adjusted to correct the change, and once normal levels are restored, the stimulus is removed. This returns the system to its set point.
